notes.meaning: God invites Israel to come back to Him for real, not halfway. That means throwing out the idols He hates and not drifting back to them again. Sin must be put away from the heart, because God sees the heart. If they truly returned, they would not be dragged off into captivity.

To swear "As surely as the LORD lives" means to worship the true God alone. It must be done honestly, fairly and rightly, never to back up a lie. If Israel turned back like this, other nations would see it. They would seek God's blessing and boast in Him. This echoes God's old promise to Abraham to bless all nations.

Now God speaks to Judah and Jerusalem. A hard heart is like a field nobody has plowed, full of thorns and weeds. Breaking it up means true repentance, which means turning from sin to God. Seed sown among thorns gets choked, just as worldly cares choke God's word in a careless heart.

Circumcision was the body sign that a man belonged to God's covenant, His binding promise-relationship with Israel. Every Jewish man had the outward sign. But God wanted their hearts cut free from sinful desires too. The sign is empty without the inner reality, as Paul also says in Romans 2:29. If they refused, God's anger would burn like a fire no one could put out, because of their own evil deeds.

Jeremiah sounds the alarm of war. People must blow the trumpet and run to the walled cities. They must raise a flag pointing to Zion, Jerusalem's strongest fortress. God is bringing disaster from the north, meaning Babylon. God usually warns before He strikes.

The lion is Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. He has already destroyed many nations, so Judah cannot hope to escape. Jeremiah speaks as if he were already on the march, to show how certain it is. The cities will be left empty.

Sackcloth was rough cloth worn in grief. The people will have nothing left to do but mourn and wail, because God's anger has not turned away. Instead of picking up swords, they will put on sackcloth. Behind the enemy's fury stands God's anger at their sin.

On that day the king and his officials will lose their courage and not know what to do. The priests will tremble. The false prophets who promised peace will be stunned. Sin takes away a person's confidence before God, and with it their courage before others.

Jeremiah cries out in grief. False prophets had promised peace in God's name, but now a sword is at the people's throats. God deceives no one. As a judgment, He let lying prophets mislead people who would not listen to the truth.

The Babylonian army is pictured as a scorching desert wind. It is not the gentle breeze farmers use to blow chaff away from grain. This wind is too strong for that, and it sweeps everything away. It comes at God's command, as God the Judge passes sentence on His people.

The enemy rolls in like storm clouds, with chariots like a whirlwind and horses faster than eagles. There is no stopping them and no outrunning them. The people cry out, "Woe to us, for we are ruined!"

Even now God calls Jerusalem to wash her heart clean so she can be saved. Outward fixes are not enough. Only a change that reaches the heart will help. "How long" shows God thinks they have waited too long, while sinful thoughts and false hopes of safety stay inside them like welcome guests.
Bad news comes first from Dan, the city in the far north. Then it comes from the hills of Ephraim, much closer to Jerusalem. The enemy is getting nearer and nearer.

An army comes from a far land to besiege Judah's cities, shouting its war cry. Like guards around a field, they will surround Jerusalem so no one can get in or out. The reason is plain: she has rebelled against God.

God says their own ways and deeds brought this on them. It is not bad luck, and it is not God's failure. Their whole way of life was wrong, not just a slip or two. The result is bitter and cuts to the heart.

Jeremiah cries out in deep pain, his heart pounding, because in his spirit he hears the trumpet of war. He takes no pleasure in his message of judgment. He grieves for his people, not for himself. True ministers feel the suffering of God's people.

One disaster follows right on the heels of another, and the whole land is ruined. The "tents" may be the homes of shepherds and country people, which were struck first. Or they may stand for the cities, which fall as easily as tents.
"How long?" asks the cry. The war would not be short. It would drag on for years. Those who love God long for peace.

God gives the reason for all this. His people are foolish and do not know Him. Yet He still calls them "My people." They are clever at doing evil but have no idea how to do good, the opposite of Romans 16:19. Knowing God is true wisdom.

"Formless and void" are the very words of Genesis 1:2. It is as if creation were being undone in the land of Judah. The dark sky shows God's displeasure. Jeremiah says "I looked" four times to make the scene hit harder.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some Bible teachers use this verse to argue that the earth became empty after a great disaster that happened between Genesis 1:1 and 1:2. Others answer that Jeremiah is only describing Judah ruined by judgment.

notes.meaning: Even the mountains, the most solid things on earth, shake and sway. This shows how fearful God is when He comes against His people. Some read the mountains as a picture of rulers trembling.
No people are left, and even the birds have flown away. The land is so ruined that there is nothing for them to eat. Sin empties a land.
The fruitful land, like rich Mount Carmel, has become a desert, and its cities lie in ruins. The invaders are not the real cause. It all happens before the LORD and His fierce anger.

The whole land will be ruined, but God will not wipe it out completely. Even in judgment He remembers mercy. He will keep a remnant, a small group of His people, and Jerusalem will be rebuilt. He may correct His people hard, but He will not throw them away.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the words "but I will not finish its destruction" were probably added later, because they break the rhythm and flow of the poem.

notes.meaning: Earth and sky are pictured as mourners dressed in black. God has spoken and planned this, and He will not take it back. The people would not turn back from their sins, so God will not turn back from His judgment.

Just the sound of horsemen and archers sends whole cities running. People hide in the bushes and climb among the rocks, and every town is left empty. We should not love our houses too much. A day may come when rocks and thickets are the safer place.

Jerusalem is pictured as a woman dressing up in scarlet, gold and eye makeup to win her lovers. This stands for her trying to buy help from other nations like Egypt. It is all in vain. Her "lovers" will turn on her and seek her life. No outward show or clever scheme can replace turning back to God.

Jerusalem's cry is like a woman in labor with her first child, which was thought the most painful birth. The "Daughter of Zion" means the people of Jerusalem. She gasps for breath and stretches out her hands for help, crying that murderers surround her. Sooner or later, sorrow finds those who feel safe in their sin.
